source_text: Ὃς δ᾽ ὑποδεξάμενος ἐξ ἡμέρας τῆς πρώτης, τῆς ὄντως ἐμοὶ πρώτης, τῆς τιμιωτάτης πασῶν, εἰ δεῖ λέγειν, ἡμερῶν, ὅτε μοι πρῶτον ὁ ἀληθινὸς ἀνατέλλειν ἥλιος ἤρξατο· πρῶτον μὲν ὥσπερ θῆράς τινας ἀγρίους ἢ ἰχθύας, ἢ τινὰς ὄρνεις, ἐμπεσόντας μὲν εἰς τὰς ἄρκυς ἢ εἰς τὰς σαγήνας, ἐξολισθαίνειν δὲ καὶ ἀποδιδράσκειν πειρωμένους, ἀναχωρεῖν τε ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ βουλομένους ἐπὶ τὴν Βηρυτὸν, ἢ ἐπὶ τὴν πατρίδα, συνδῆσαι πάντα τρόπον ἐμηχανήσατο· πάντας λόγους στρέφων, καὶ πάντα κάλων, τὸ δὴ τοῦ λόγου, κινῶν, καὶ πάσας τὰς δυνάμεις προσχειριζόμενος. ἐπαινῶν μὲν φιλοσοφίαν, καὶ τοὺς φιλοσοφίας ἐραστὰς, μακροῖς τοῖς ἐπαίνοις καὶ πολλοῖς τισί τε προσήκουσι, τούτους μόνους ζῆν ὄντως τὸν λογικοῖς προσήκοντα βίον, λέγων, τοὺς ὀρθῶς βιοῦν ἐπιτηδεύοντας, ἑαυτούς τε γινώσκοντας πρῶτον οἵτινές εἰσι· κἄπειτα τὰ ὄντως ἀγαθὰ ἃ μεταδιώκειν ἄνθρωπον χρὴ, καὶ τὰ ἀληθῶς κακὰ ὧν ἀποφεύγειν δεῖ. ψέγων δὲ τὴν ἀμαθίαν, καὶ πάντας τοὺς ἀμαθεῖς· πολλοὶ δὲ οὗτοι ὅσοι θρεμμάτων δίκην τυφλώττοντες τὸν νοῦν, οὐδ᾽ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ὅπερ εἰσὶν, ἐγνωκότες, ὥσπερ ἄλογοι πεπλανημένοι, ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακὸν ὅ, τι ποτέ ἐστιν, ὅλως οὔτε εἰδότες αὐτοὶ, οὔτε μαθεῖν θέλοντες, ὡς ἐπὶ ἀγαθὸν ἄττουσι καὶ ἐπτόηνται, χρήματα καὶ δόξας καὶ τιμὰς τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν πολλῶν καὶ τὴν τοῦ σώματος εὐεξίαν· αὐτά τε περὶ πολλοῦ καὶ τοῦ παντὸς τεθέμενοι, καὶ τῶν τεχνῶν ὅσαι ταῦτα ἐκπορίζεσθαι δύνανται, καὶ τῶν βίων ὅσοι ταῦτα παρέξονται, στρατείας καὶ τὴν δικανικὴν καὶ τὴν ἐκμάθησιν τῶν νόμων. ταῦθ᾽ ἅπερ ἡμᾶς ἀνέσειε, μάλιστα λέγων καὶ μάλα τεχνικῶς, τοῦ κυριωτάτου φησὶ τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν λόγου ἀμελήσαντας· οὐκ ἔχω νῦν ἐγὼ λέγειν, ὅσας τοιαύτας ἐξήνεγκε φωνὰς προτρέπων φιλοσοφεῖν· οὐ μιᾶς ἡμέρας μόνης, ἀλλὰ καὶ πλειόνων ὅσων αὐτῷ προσῄειμεν τῶν πρώτων, βεβλημένοι μὲν ὥσπερ τινὶ βέλει τῷ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ καὶ ἐκ πρώτης ἡλικίας. ἦν γάρ πως καὶ ἡδείᾳ τινὶ χάριτι καὶ πειθοῖ καί τινι ἀνάγκῃ μεμιγμένος. στρεφόμενοι δέ πως ἔτι καὶ λογιζόμενοι, καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν μὲν προσκαρτερήσαντες, οὐδέπω πάντῃ πεπεισμένοι· ἀφίστασθαι δὲ πάλιν οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως οὐ δυνάμενοι· ἀεὶ δὲ ὥσπερ ὑπό τισιν ἀνάγκαις μείζοσι τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἑλκόμενοι.
orientation: From the first day Origen works to hold the young men and urges them toward philosophy.
pass_a_gloss: Who, having received (hypodexamenos) [us] from the first day, the truly first for me, the most precious (timiotate) of all days, if one must say, when for me first the true sun (alethinos helios) began to rise (anatellein): first, like some wild beasts (theres agrioi) or fish or some birds, having fallen into the snares (arkyes) or into the dragnets (sagenai), but trying to slip out (exolisthainein) and run away, and wishing to withdraw from him to Berytus or to the homeland (patris), he contrived (emechanesato) in every way to bind [us] together (syndesai): turning all arguments (logoi), and moving every rope (kalos), as the saying goes, and putting all his powers (dynameis) to hand. Praising philosophy (philosophia) and the lovers (erastai) of philosophy with long and many and fitting praises, saying that these alone truly live the life befitting rational beings (logikoi), those practicing (epitedeuontas) to live rightly (orthos bioun), knowing themselves first, who they are; and then the truly good things which a man must pursue, and the truly evil things which one must flee. And blaming (psegon) ignorance (amathia) and all the ignorant: and many are these, who in the manner of cattle (thremmata) being blind (typhlottontes) in mind (nous), not having known even this very thing, what they are, like unreasoning [creatures] wandering, neither knowing at all themselves what good or evil is, nor wishing to learn, as toward a good dart (attousi) and are excited (eptoentai) at money, glories (doxai), honors from the many, and the good condition (euexia) of the body; having set these at much, and at everything, and of the arts, as many as can provide these, and of the ways of life (bioi), as many as will furnish these: military service (strateia), pleading (dikanike), and the learning of the laws. Saying most of all and very artfully (technikos) these things which shook us up (anesei): [us] having neglected, he says, the most sovereign (kyriotatos) of the things in us, reason (logos). I cannot now say how many such utterances (phonai) he brought out, urging [us] to philosophize (protrepon philosophein); not on one day only, but on more, as many of the first as we came to him, struck (beblemenoi) as by some arrow (belos) by the word from him, even from the first age (helikia). For it was somehow mixed with a certain sweet grace (charis) and persuasion (peitho) and a certain compulsion (ananke). But still turning about somehow and reasoning, and persevering (proskarteresantes) in philosophizing, not yet wholly persuaded; yet unable, I know not how, to stand off again; but always drawn toward him by his words as by some greater compulsions.

pass_b_english: He received us from the first day, truly the first day for me, the most precious of all my days, if I may say so, when the true sun first began to rise on me. At first we were like wild beasts, or fish, or birds that have fallen into snares or nets and try to slip out and run away: we wanted to leave him for Berytus or for our homeland. But he contrived in every way to bind us, turning every argument, moving every rope, as the proverb has it, and bringing all his powers to bear. He praised philosophy and the lovers of philosophy with long and many and fitting praises. He said that they alone truly live the life fit for rational beings who take care to live rightly, knowing first of all themselves, what they are, and then the things that are truly good, which a human being must pursue, and the things that are truly evil, which one must flee.

He censured ignorance and all the ignorant. And there are many of them: people blind in mind like cattle, who do not know even what they themselves are, who wander like creatures without reason, neither knowing at all what good or evil is, nor willing to learn. As if toward the good, they rush and flutter after money, fame, honors from the crowd, and bodily health. They prize these highly, indeed as everything, and with them the arts that can provide them and the ways of life that will supply them: soldiering, pleading in the courts, and the study of law. He spoke most of all, and with great skill, about these very things that had stirred us, saying that we had neglected what is most sovereign in us, reason.

I cannot now tell how many such appeals he made, urging us to study philosophy, not on one day only but on many, as many as we came to him in those first days. We were struck by his word as by an arrow from the very first, for it was blended with a certain sweet grace and persuasion, and with a kind of compulsion. Yet we still wavered and kept reasoning it over. We kept at philosophy, though we were not yet wholly persuaded; but somehow we could not draw back again, and we were always being drawn to him by his words, as if by some greater compulsion.
notes: 'Moving every rope, as the proverb has it' keeps Gregory's sailing proverb (panta kalon kinein, to use every means). 'He spoke most of all, and with great skill, about these very things that had stirred us, saying that we had neglected' renders the doubtful 'tauth' haper hemas anesei, malista legon kai mala technikos' (verb split over a line and partly blurred); Koetschau prints the same verb; phesi ('he says') goes with 'having neglected'; the Latin column takes it as 'these make us idle and slothful', so the verb is uncertain, but both readings blame these pursuits. 'From the very first' renders ek protes helikias, literally 'from the first age'; the phrase is odd in context, and later editions may read a different noun; the English keeps the sense 'from the start'. 'Snares or nets' renders arkyes (hunting nets) and sagenai (dragnets). Allusions left uncited: 'the true sun' may recall the sun of righteousness (Malachi 4:2), and the dragnet image may recall Matthew 13:47, but neither is quoted; they are taken as Gregory's own figures.
